unit.title: Place Value and Rounding
unit.blurb: Multiplying and dividing whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, and rounding to the nearest power of 10 and to decimal places.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Multiply and divide integers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, using place value.

O2.t: Round numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 and to a given number of decimal places.

sections.title: Multiplying and dividing by powers of 10

lesson.t: What happens when I multiply or divide by a power of 10?
p: 10, 100, 1000 are **powers of 10** (10¹, 10², 10³). Each place in our number system is worth 10 times the place to its right.
So **× 10** moves every digit **1 place left**, × 100 two places, × 1000 three places. **÷ 10** moves every digit **1 place right**, and so on.
The decimal point stays still; the digits move. Empty places up to the point are filled with 0.
Multiplying by 0.1 is the same as dividing by 10 (0.1 = 1/10). Dividing by 0.1 is the same as multiplying by 10.

lesson.t: How do I multiply or divide by 10, 100, 1000?
p: Step 1: Count the zeros (that is the number of places).
Step 2: × → digits move left (bigger); ÷ → digits move right (smaller).
Step 3: Fill gaps with 0 and check the size makes sense.

steps: 45 → 0.045: the 4 moves from tens to hundredths

p: 3.8 × 10 is 38, not 3.80. 'Add a zero' only works for whole numbers – think about moving digits instead.
× makes bigger, ÷ makes smaller (for powers of 10). Check your answer against this every time.

p: **Rounding** gives an approximate value that is easier to use. We round to the nearest 10, 100, 1000 or to a number of **decimal places (d.p.)**.
4372 to the nearest 100 is 4400, because 4372 is closer to 4400 than to 4300.

lesson.t: How do I decide whether to round up or down?
p: Look at the **decider** – the digit just after the place you are rounding to.
**5 or more → round up; 4 or less → round down.**
The number of **decimal places** is the number of digits after the decimal point. 3.142 has 3 d.p.
Rounding to 1 d.p. means keeping one digit after the point; to 2 d.p., two digits.

lesson.t: How do I round to a given number of decimal places?
p: Step 1: Count that many digits after the decimal point and draw a line after the last one.
Step 2: Look at the digit after the line (the decider).
Step 3: 5 or more → add 1 to the digit before the line; 4 or less → leave it.
Step 4: Remove everything after the line. Keep zeros needed to show the decimal places.

steps: only the digit straight after the line counts

p: 19.97 to 1 d.p. is **20.0**, not 20. The 0 shows that the answer is correct to 1 d.p.
Draw a small line after the last digit you keep. Then you look only at the decider – never round twice.
